cls: Atypical tricyclic-related antidepressant with mu-opioid receptor agonist activity
pharm: Modulates glutamatergic neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity and acts as a full agonist at the mu-opioid receptor; this opioid activity underlies its abuse and dependence potential
quick: 12.5 mg three times daily (therapeutic dose where approved); NOT an FDA-approved dose
Usually taken before meals per regional product information
No dose change usually needed; caution in severe impairment
Caution; reduce dose per regional product information
summary: Tianeptine is an atypical antidepressant available in some European, Asian, and Latin American countries (typically 12.5 mg three times daily) for major depression. It is NOT FDA-approved and is increasingly recognized as a drug of abuse because of mu-opioid receptor agonism, with reports of dependence, withdrawal, and overdose. High supratherapeutic doses sold in unregulated products are associated with serious harm.
indications: Treatment of major depressive disorder / depressive states (in countries where approved; per regional product information)
NOT FDA-approved for any indication in the United States

dosage.d: 12.5 mg orally three times daily (standard therapeutic dose)
dosage.n: Regional therapeutic dose only; not FDA-defined. Doses far above this seen in misuse are dangerous

admin: Take orally before meals as directed by the regional product information
Do not exceed the recommended therapeutic dose - higher doses carry serious abuse and overdose risk
Do not stop abruptly; taper to avoid withdrawal
moa: Tianeptine has an unusual pharmacology among antidepressants. It modulates glutamatergic AMPA/NMDA signaling and enhances neuronal plasticity and stress resilience. It is also a full agonist at the mu-opioid receptor (and to a lesser extent the delta-opioid receptor); this opioid activity is believed to contribute to both its antidepressant-like effects and its potential for euphoria, abuse, dependence, and withdrawal.

absolute: Concomitant use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
relative: History of substance use disorder or opioid dependence (high misuse risk)
monitor: Mood and suicidality, especially early in treatment and in young adults
Signs of misuse, escalating use, or dependence/withdrawal

preg: Safety in pregnancy has not been established. Use is generally avoided during pregnancy; given its mu-opioid activity, late-pregnancy exposure could pose a risk of neonatal effects. Follow regional product information and specialist advice.
lact: It is not known whether tianeptine is safe during breastfeeding; data are insufficient. Use is generally avoided during lactation.
renal: Dose adjustment is generally not required for renal impairment per regional product information; use caution in severe impairment.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; a reduced dose (e.g. 12.5 mg twice daily) is recommended in the elderly and may be appropriate with significant hepatic impairment per regional product information.

major: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors - contraindicated (risk of serotonergic/hypertensive reactions)
Opioids and other CNS depressants (including alcohol, benzodiazepines) - additive sedation and respiratory depression
moderate: Other serotonergic agents - theoretical serotonin-related effects
interactions.food: Usually taken before meals per regional product information
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive central nervous system and opioid-type depression
interactions.diagnostics: May be detected on some opioid-related testing; abuse may be missed on standard panels

serious: Dependence, tolerance, and opioid-type withdrawal on stopping
emergency: Opioid-type overdose: sedation, respiratory depression, coma (especially at supratherapeutic/abused doses)
Severe withdrawal syndrome (agitation, tachycardia, GI symptoms)

monitoring: Mood, depressive symptoms, and suicidality (especially early and in young adults)
Signs of misuse, dose escalation, or dependence
Liver function if hepatotoxicity is suspected
counsel: Take only the prescribed therapeutic dose - higher amounts can cause opioid-like effects, dependence, and dangerous overdose
Do not stop suddenly; your clinician will taper the dose to avoid withdrawal
Report worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm immediately
Be aware that unregulated 'supplement' products containing high-dose tianeptine are unsafe
pk: Rapidly absorbed orally with peak plasma concentrations within about 1-2 hours
Short elimination half-life of approximately 2.5 to 3 hours (drives three-times-daily therapeutic dosing)
Short-acting; the brief half-life contributes to frequent redosing and misuse patterns
Store as directed on the product packaging
pearls: Tianeptine is NOT FDA-approved in the US; it is approved as an antidepressant (typically 12.5 mg three times daily) in some other countries. Dosing here reflects regional product information
It is a full mu-opioid receptor agonist - the basis for its recognized abuse, dependence, withdrawal, and overdose potential ('gas station heroin' in unregulated products)
Contraindicated with MAOIs; avoid combining with opioids, alcohol, or other CNS depressants
Opioid-type overdose may respond to naloxone; severe respiratory depression should be treated as an opioid overdose
Several US states have scheduled or banned tianeptine; counsel patients against unregulated high-dose products
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, then skip it - do not double up. Do not stop the medicine abruptly because of withdrawal risk; discuss any changes with your clinician.
overdose: Overdose, particularly at the high supratherapeutic doses seen in misuse, can cause opioid-type toxicity with profound sedation, respiratory depression, and coma. Manage as an opioid overdose: support airway and ventilation, and consider naloxone (repeat dosing may be needed given the short half-life). Provide supportive care, monitor cardiorespiratory status, and contact a poison control center.
